recipe.history:
Swiss Emmentaler cheese is one of the most iconic and imitated cheeses in the world, originating in the Emme valley of the canton of Bern in Switzerland, with a documented history stretching back to the thirteenth century. The cheese's defining characteristic — its large, regular holes, called eyes, formed by carbon dioxide produced by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria during the aging process — made it visually distinctive and contributed to its global recognition. True Emmentaler AOP (Appellation d'Origine Protégée) is produced from raw cow's milk in Switzerland's traditional alpine dairies, where the combination of specific bacterial cultures, raw mountain milk, and traditional copper vat production creates a cheese of characteristic nutty, slightly sweet, and delicate flavor. Young Emmentaler, aged only a few months, is milder and creamier than the sharp, complex aged varieties; it melts with extraordinary smoothness, making it one of the great melting cheeses in the world and the traditional basis for Swiss fondue. The word congeniality — warmth, friendliness, pleasant agreeableness — could not be better applied to a cheese: Emmentaler is the affable diplomat of the cheese world, getting along with everyone and refusing to cause offense.

Swiss cheese, as Americans know it, is almost entirely a reflection of Emmentaler and its imitators — the domestic Swiss produced in Wisconsin, Ohio, and New York that arrived with Swiss and German immigrant cheesemakers in the nineteenth century. It became a fixture of American deli culture, appearing in Reuben sandwiches, club sandwiches, and as the default cheese for any preparation where a mild, melty option was called for. Its role on the hamburger is both humble and essential: Swiss melts over a patty in translucent, lacy pools, adding a subtle nuttiness and a creamy richness without overwhelming the beef's natural flavor. A burger that celebrates Swiss cheese is a burger that values harmony over drama — a burger that wants everything to work together in quiet, gracious unison. The Swiss Congeniality Burger is the pleasant, well-liked neighbor of the burger menu, the one that everyone gets along with and that quietly turns out to be the most satisfying thing you ate all week.

I made this burger on an ordinary Wednesday when I did not feel like thinking too hard about what I wanted to eat, and the Swiss Congeniality Burger was the result of having good ingredients and a respect for their simplicity. I had beautiful young Emmentaler from the cheese shop, a ripe tomato, some crisp butter lettuce, a sourdough roll I had baked the day before, and a batch of homemade Thousand Island dressing that I had been working through all week. I shaped the patty, seared it in cast iron until it had that crust I cannot live without, draped two slices of Emmentaler over it and watched them melt into each other in slow, glossy, lacy folds. On the bun, the dressing, the lettuce, the tomato. The patty with its veil of Swiss. The top bun. I ate it at the table, with a glass of cold beer, and it was exactly what I needed — no drama, no surprises, nothing fighting for attention. Everything in its right place. Sometimes that is the most satisfying burger of all.

Medium rare is the standard by which all burgers are judged, and this applies with particular truth to the Swiss Congeniality Burger, precisely because its character is built on balance and restraint. Young Emmentaler is a gentle cheese — its flavor is mild, its melt is silky, and it depends on the patty beneath it to provide the richness and depth that the cheese itself does not supply in abundance. A medium rare patty at 130–135°F (54–57°C) is the backbone this cheese needs: its fat content fully present, its moisture retained, its flavor deep and beefy without being aggressive. The Swiss melts over a medium rare patty into something that feels almost like a sauce — it pools and flows and mingles with the crust juices, creating a union that a dry, well-done patty with its absent moisture could never achieve. The congeniality of this burger depends entirely on the good character of the medium rare patty beneath it — take that away, and there is nothing left to be congenial about.
ingredients: 1 tbsp apple cider vinegar (for mild sour flavor)
1 large egg plus 1 for egg wash
12 slices young Swiss Emmentaler cheese (2 per burger — mild and melty)
1 small white onion, sliced into thin rings
Yellow mustard (optional, for the top bun)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine yeast, warm water, warm milk, sugar, and apple cider vinegar; let sit 5–10 minutes until foamy. Combine flours and salt in a stand mixer. Add yeast mixture, egg, and softened butter. Knead with dough hook 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

2. Rise in an oiled covered bowl 1–1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 6 portions, shape into tight rounds, and proof on a parchment-lined baking sheet covered loosely for 45 minutes until puffed. Brush with egg wash and bake at 375°F for 16–18 minutes until golden. Cool completely.

3. Make the Thousand Island dressing: Combine mayonnaise, ketchup, sweet pickle relish, minced onion, apple cider vinegar, Worcestershire sauce, paprika, salt, and white pepper. Stir until fully combined. Taste and adjust seasoning — it should be creamy, sweet, tangy, and slightly savory. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld.

4. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 6 portions (about 4 oz each). Form gently into patties about 3/4 inch thick, pressing a shallow dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and onion powder. Refrigerate 15 minutes before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until just beginning to smoke. Add neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place patties dimple-side up and cook undisturbed 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once, immediately lay 2 slices of young Swiss Emmentaler on each patty, and cook 2–3 more minutes. For extra-melty cheese, place a stainless steel bowl or pan lid over the patties with a splash of water in the pan to create steam for the final 30–45 seconds. Cook until internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3–4 minutes tented loosely with foil.
6. Toast the buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until lightly golden.

7. Assemble: Spread a generous spoonful of Thousand Island dressing on both bun halves. Place a large leaf of butter lettuce on the bottom bun. Add a slice or two of ripe tomato. Place the rested, double Swiss-topped patty on the tomato. Layer a few thin rings of white onion over the cheese. Add 2–3 pickle slices. Spread a thin line of yellow mustard on the top bun if desired. Crown the burger with the top bun and serve immediately while the cheese is still glossy and molten.
